title: Countable and uncountable: some, any, much, many
tagline: How many apples, how much juice: countable and uncountable nouns.
why: Every shopping list, recipe and conversation about money needs this: is it something you can count (apples, friends), or something you can't (water, homework)? Get it wrong and much/many, a few/a little come out backwards — a very common mistake the exam checks in Reading Parts 5 and 6.

hook.text: Miss Vega is making a shopping list for the party. "How many apples do we need?" she asks. "Ten!" says Sofia. "And how much juice?" Mateo thinks: "A lot — we're always thirsty after football!"
hook.ask: Many goes with apples, much goes with juice. Can you work out why they're different words?

branches.label: some / any
items: not any apples / not any water

branches.label: much / many
items: a lot of works for both

diagrams.title: How to ask about quantity

steps.label: Countable → use How many + plural noun

diagrams.caption: Same question, different word — it all depends on whether you can count the noun.

rows.label: Making it countable
cells: a piece of cake, a bottle of water

use.point: Countable nouns: you can count them

examples.text: I've got two apples in my bag.
How many friends do you have in this school?

use.point: Uncountable nouns: no plural, no a/an

examples.text: I don't have much money this week.
We've got a lot of homework tonight.
Can you give me some information about the trip?
There are some apples on the table.
Is there any water in the fridge?

examples.note: some in offers, even though it's a question

use.point: How much / how many, a lot of, a few, a little, containers

examples.note: a few = a small number, countable

examples.text: Can I have a piece of cake and a bottle of water?

watch_out.why: Homework is uncountable: no plural, no many.

watch_out.wrong: How much apples do you want?
watch_out.why: Apples is countable, so use many, not much.

watch_out.wrong: Can I have any water? (as an offer)
watch_out.why: Offers usually use some, even in a question.
A few is for countable nouns; a little is for uncountable nouns.
Information is uncountable: no a/an, no plural.

l1.why: Money is uncountable in English, even though dinero can feel countable in Spanish.
Homework has no plural in English.

l1.wrong: How many information do you have?
l1.why: Information is uncountable, so it takes much, not many.
Advice is uncountable in English — no a/an, no plural.

remember.trick: Count it? many/few. Can't count it? much/little!
remember.tip: If you can put a number before it (two apples), it's countable → many/few. If you can't (money, water), it's uncountable → much/little.

dialogue.title: Shopping for the class party
dialogue.context: Miss Vega and the students make a shopping list for the end-of-term party.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: How many apples do we need for the party?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I think ten apples is enough. But how much juice should we buy?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We need a lot of juice — everyone's thirsty after the football match!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Have we got any cups? I can't see any in the box.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: There are some plates, but we need a few more cups.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. And a piece of advice: buy a bottle of water for every table.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Is there any money left for a cake?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes, we've got a little money — enough for one big cake.

can_do: I can tell countable nouns (apple, friend) from uncountable nouns (money, homework).
I can use some and any correctly in statements, questions and offers.
I can ask How many…? and How much…? and answer with a few, a little or a lot of.
summary: Countable nouns have a plural (apples, friends); uncountable nouns don't (money, homework, information).
Use some in statements and offers, any in questions and negatives.
Ask How many + plural noun, or How much + uncountable noun.
A few and many go with countable nouns; a little and much go with uncountable nouns — but a lot of works with both.
